title: Archival FEROS and ESPRESSO spectra (2015-2025) show that the Be star of HD 93683 orbits the eclipsing pair every 891 days; this orbit can cause the loss of the eclipses
abstract: Prior campaign studies found that the eclipses of HD 93683 (a 17.8-day eclipsing binary with a Be-type star in its spectrum) faded from 1990 to 2026 because the inner orbit tilts by -0.33 deg/yr. They predicted a third body with an outer period below about 4.3 years and asked for radial velocities. We measured 22 public ESO FEROS and ESPRESSO spectra from 2015 to 2025. Thirteen Fe II emission lines of the Be-star disc give a Keplerian orbit with P2 = 891.3 +- 0.6 d, e2 = 0.346 +- 0.007, K = 59.18 +- 0.41 km/s and mass function 15.80 +- 0.29 solar masses (rms 0.64 km/s). Interstellar lines stay constant to 1.15 km/s. Fourier disentangling of three stars shows that the systemic velocity of the eclipsing pair moves in anti-phase with the Be star. The coupling ratio q = m3/(m1+m2) is 0.59 (window jackknife error 0.17; 0.42 to 0.78 for different line sets), and the physical limit from the mass function is 0.615. A leave-one-out test gives the anti-phase motion also with component spectra built under no coupling. The pair has K1 = 144 and K2 = 147 km/s, so m1 + m2 is about 41 solar masses and the Be star has about 16-25 solar masses. In quadrupole dynamics this outer orbit can tilt the inner orbit by up to 0.66 deg/yr; the observed rate needs a mutual inclination near 15-21 deg or 75 deg (or retrograde mirrors). Thus the Be star is the third body that the eclipse history requires. Limitations: q and the masses depend on the line set; the Fe II emission is assumed to trace the Be star (absorption-line scale test 1.008); TESS eclipse times from the source study do not fit any tested ephemeris and cannot test the predicted 22-minute light-travel-time delay; public VLTI/GRAVITY data (2022-2024) were not reduced. We give predicted separations at the GRAVITY epochs for that test.
